procedural_history.impugned_order: Conviction under sections 353 and 506(1) of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State appealed the Magistrate Court's decision to the High Court under s. 417 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The High Court allowed the appeal and convicted Mangat Rai under s. 353 and s. 506 (1), sentencing him to rigorous imprisonment for four months on each count, the sentences to run concurrently.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Mangat Rai appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's decision. He contended that the Act did not authorize forcible inspection of accounts and that the Inspector was exercising powers of seizure under s. 29(3) of the Act which he did not have. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails and is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Sales Tax Inspector, under the Madhya Pradesh General Sales-Tax Act, 1958, is entitled to remove an obstruction to inspect account books, or if the Act only contemplates voluntary submission to inspection.

facts: A Sales Tax Inspector visited the appellant's shop for a surprise check and wanted to inspect his account books.
An attempt was made to remove the account books from the shop in a clandestine manner to prevent the inspection.
The Inspector tried to forcibly take possession of the books to prevent their removal and to carry out the inspection.
law: Under Section 29(2) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales-Tax Act, 1958, all accounts of a dealer shall be open to inspection.
Section 29(4) of the Act empowers the relevant officer to search any place of business for the purpose of inspection.
The appellant argued that the Act only contemplates voluntary submission to inspection and does not permit an inspector to use force.
The appellant contended that the Inspector's actions amounted to an illegal "seizure" under Section 29(3), a power the Inspector did not have.
application: The Court reasoned that if it accepted the appellant's argument, the powers of inspection and search under the Act would be nullified, as any dealer could simply snatch away books to avoid inspection.

The Court distinguished the Inspector's actions from a "seizure." It held that the Inspector's goal was not to permanently dispossess the trader of the books, but only to hold them temporarily for inspection.
The Court found that the power to search business premises for the purpose of inspection implies the power to get hold of the account books.

Therefore, when the Inspector saw the books and forcibly tried to take them, he was not attempting an illegal seizure but was lawfully attempting to enforce his right of inspection and execute his duties.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that a Sales Tax Inspector is entitled to remove an obstruction to inspect account books. The Court concluded that the Inspector's attempt to forcibly take the books for a temporary inspection was a legitimate part of executing his duties and did not amount to an illegal seizure.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Sales Tax Inspector's act of forcibly taking possession of the account books for inspection amounted to an unauthorized 'seizure' under s. 29(3) of the Act.

facts: A Sales Tax Inspector visited the appellant's shop for a surprise check and wanted to inspect his account books.
When the Inspector tried to prevent the books from being removed, he forcibly attempted to take possession of them for inspection.
The appellant contended that this act was an unauthorized 'seizure' under s. 29(3) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, as the Inspector did not have the power to seize.
The appellant was convicted for using criminal force against the Inspector during this incident.
law: Section 29(2) of the Act states that a dealer's account books shall be open to inspection by the Commissioner.
Section 29(4) of the Act empowers the Commissioner to search a dealer's business premises for the purpose of conducting an inspection under s. 29(2).
Section 29(3) of the Act provides for the 'seizure' of account books.
application: The Court reasoned that the power to inspect (s. 29(2)) and the power to search for books for inspection (s. 29(4)) would be nullified if an inspector could not take hold of the books.
It distinguished between 'inspection' and 'seizure'. The Court defined 'seizure' under s. 29(3) as an act of dispossessing the trader and taking the books away from their possession.
In contrast, the Inspector's action was merely an attempt to hold the books for a temporary period for the purpose of an on-the-spot inspection.
The Court determined that the Inspector's objective was not to dispossess the trader (which would be a seizure), but to enforce his right of inspection.
Therefore, the act of forcibly taking the books for a temporary look was considered an inherent part of the power of inspection, not an exercise of the power of seizure.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the Sales Tax Inspector's act of forcibly taking possession of the account books was not an unauthorized 'seizure' under s. 29(3). Instead, it was a legitimate attempt to enforce his right of inspection, as the object was not to dispossess the trader but to hold the books temporarily for that purpose.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Sales Tax Inspector, under the Madhya Pradesh General Sales-Tax Act, 1958, is entitled to remove an obstruction to inspect account books, or if the Act only contemplates voluntary submission to inspection.
appellant_arguments: The Act only contemplates voluntary submission to inspection; there cannot be any forcible inspection of accounts.
If there is an obstruction to inspection, the only remedy is to punish the obstructor under s. 46(h) of the Act.
The Sales Tax Inspector is not empowered to use force to inspect the accounts.
respondent_arguments: The power of inspection under s. 29(2) would be nullified if an assessee could simply snatch away books to prevent inspection.
The power to inspect implies the power to overcome obstruction, otherwise, the Inspector would be left helpless.
The Inspector was acting in the execution of his duty when he tried to inspect the books, and the appellant's son was committing an offence under s. 46(h) by obstructing him.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Sales Tax Inspector's act of forcibly taking possession of the account books for inspection amounted to an unauthorized 'seizure' under s. 29(3) of the Act.
appellant_arguments: The Sales Tax Inspector's actions constituted an attempt to exercise the power of seizure under s. 29(3) of the Act.
It is common ground that the Sales Tax Inspector did not have the power to act under s. 29(3), making his actions an unauthorized seizure.
respondent_arguments: The Inspector did not perform a 'seizure'; he merely picked up the books which were lying in the shop for inspection.
The Inspector did not take the books by force; on the contrary, the books were taken away from him by force by the appellant.
The Inspector's action was part of a lawful inspection, not a seizure.

statutes.act_name: Madras General Sales Tax Act (1 of 1959)

cases.case_name: Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Ramkishan Shrikishan Jhaver
cases.principle: To show that there is no rule that provisions granting powers of inspection to tax officers should be construed very strictly, and that the power to inspect can imply a power to search for the items to be inspected.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The statutory power to enter and search a premises for the purpose of inspection includes the authority to search for and take temporary possession of account books for that inspection. This act of taking temporary possession for inspection does not constitute a 'seizure', which is defined as taking the books into possession and removing them from the premises and the assessee's control.
obiter: There is no rule that statutory provisions authorizing search and inspection should be construed very strictly.
If, indeed, he had retrieved them by force it may have been possible to urge that latter act of his amounts to seizure.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The statutory power of inspection granted to a Sales Tax Inspector under s. 29(2) of the Act is not limited to voluntary submission by the assessee. It implicitly includes the authority to overcome physical obstruction to that inspection, such as an attempt to snatch away account books, in order to prevent the power of inspection from being nullified. This act of enforcing the right to inspect is distinct from an unauthorized seizure.
legal_tests_applied: Purposive Statutory Interpretation: The court interpreted the power of 'inspection' by considering the legislative intent and the practical consequences, concluding that the power would be rendered meaningless if it did not include the ability to overcome obstruction.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the Act only contemplates voluntary inspection, reasoning that such an interpretation would nullify the statutory power of inspection and search.
The court determined that the Sales Tax Inspector's action was not an unauthorized 'seizure' under s. 29(3), but rather an attempt to enforce his legitimate right of inspection under s. 29(2).

The court found that because the Inspector was lawfully executing his duty, the appellant's son was committing an offense by obstructing him, which negated any claim of a right to private defense for the appellant.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed that the power of inspection would be nullified if an assessee could simply snatch away books to prevent it.
The court concluded that the Sales Tax Inspector was acting in the execution of his duty when he attempted to inspect the books.

The court distinguished the Inspector's actions from a seizure, noting he "merely picked up the books which were lying in the shop" and that it was the appellant who used force to take them away from the Inspector.
policy_considerations: If the power of inspection did not include the power to overcome obstruction, "Any assessee who does not want to show any particular book or if he finds that the Sales Tax Inspector has got hold of a book, which might prove damaging to his case, the assessee could snatch away or ask his clerk or son or relation to snatch away the book and run away leaving the Sales Tax Inspector helpless to do anything in the matter."
To accept the appellant's contention would be to "be nullifying the power of inspection and search contained ins. 29(2) and (4) of the Act."
